title: Daily X narrative digest — 2026-11-04

hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.text:
running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian

my team is 50+ people in 12 countries, but i talk to my agents more than my human teammates

- voice note to grokbot
- mattpocock/skills /grill-me so the agent interrogates the idea before anything gets built
- spec drops into linear through the linear mcp
- exa + firecrawl agent reads every competitor site, pricing page and changelog
- https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA to find ideas and trends
- apify pulls g2, reddit and app store reviews
- prompt: "find the 10 complaints that show up most and quote the users"
- context7 so the agent reads the latest docs before it touches any api

the design

- claude code + paper mcp
- 4 versions of every screen before a single line of code
- pick pieces from 2, it merges them. diverge then converge
- frontend-design skill from anthropic/skills + our own design system skill
- cleanshot screenshots of any ui i like go straight in with "make it feel like this"

the build

- pingdotgg/t3code as the control surface for every agent, from my phone too
- stablyai/orca runs a fleet of agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree
- graphify maps the whole codebase into a knowledge graph so agents navigate instead of guess
- headroom compresses tool outputs before they hit the model, so tokens go 20-95% further
- lsp plugins so the agent sees types and errors like an ide does
- security guidance hook flags risky edits before they land
- supabase mcp for the database, stripe for billing
- github mcp opens the pr, vercel spins up a preview
- loops run overnight, i check what shipped over coffee

the user testing

- lightpanda as the headless browser, way lighter than chromium so you can run hundreds at once
- agents click every flow on the preview like a first-time user
- one persona is impatient, one is confused, one is on a phone
- playwright + chrome devtools mcp for regression tests

the bugs

- sentry mcp catches the error
- agent reads the stack trace and opens a fix pr in under 10 minutes
- human just approves

the data

- posthog mcp cron at 7am on yesterday's funnel
- any step that drops more than 10%, the agent watches 20 session replays and tells me why
- stripe mcp pulls every cancellation reason into one doc every monday

the agents' tools

- orgo so every agent gets its own computer
- agentmail so every agent gets its own inbox
- agentphone so i can call them from the car
- composio connect-apps for every other connector
- akitaonrails/ai-memory, a git-backed markdown wiki so they remember what we decided last week

the skills

- wshobson/agents so skills work across claude code, codex and opencode
- my writing voice
- our design system
- how we write specs
- skill creator so the agents write new skills themselves

some helpful tricks

- one agent per platform. the x agent never touches email
- cheap model for triage, opus for anything that ships
- every output gets scored 1-10 by an llm judge. under 8 goes back
- every agent writes a 5-line log at night so i can read the whole company in 2 minutes
- every agent mistake becomes a new skill, so it only happens once

the team

- humans get version 5, not my voice note which they are happy about lol 
- their job is creative feedback, relationships and telling the agents what they got wrong

a human pm reviews the funnel once a week. this reviews it every morning

running a company is now voice notes and inference
hits.hook: running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian  my team is 50+ people in 12 countries, but i talk to my agents more th
hits.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg runs a 50+ person company across 12 countries and says he now talks to his agents more than his teammates. 519k views, 12.8k bookmarks.

His whole stack is in the post: a voice note to Grok Bot, an agent that interrogates the idea before anything gets built, four versions of every screen before code, a fleet of agents in separate git worktrees, Sentry errors turned into fix PRs, and every agent writing a 5-line log each night.

The rule worth copying first: every agent mistake becomes a new skill, so it only happens once.
hits.video_tip: 12s: phone voice note, then a fast montage of spec, screens, PR, preview, caption 'voice note to shipped feature'.

hits.name: @levelsio
hits.text:
💸 Update: My total biz expenses have now dropped to just ~$300/mo!

This is to run all my websites/apps serving per year:
- 20,000 paying customers
- 252 million visitors
- 2.4 billion requests
- 2.4 petabyte (PB) in bandwidth

(~$8,000/mo if you add the $7,000/mo GPU bill and $800/mo R2 storage I pay for Photo AI, I exclude it above because it's one project that's so much more expensive in size than all the other sites together, but included in the chart below)

Claude Code helped me to find smart ways to save more money, AI is just really really really good at finding cost savings by itself, which is not so great for the economy short-term, but long term it trims all the fat and opens up spending for better investments I think

Anyway here's what it saved me in money, almost $34,000/mo:

- $29,000/mo - switched to better and cheaper video models on Photo AI, video was very expensive and since I didn't update it ever it stayed expensive, also routed some image jobs to Google Cloud where I have some Google Cloud Credits, and also routed some jobs to Sume which sells AI models at market cost, very cool! This made my GPU bill go from $36,000/mo to $7,000/mo

- $3,000/mo - consolidated my servers, cancelled Digital Ocean and Linode and moved everything to Hetzner saving about $3,000/mo

- $1100/mo - analyzed my Backblaze B2 server backups, I had infinite versioning and lifecycle policies, that's reduced now to 30 days, this literally pushed the bill from $1,200/mo to $26/mo, about 50x cheaper! I had essentially versions of files for all my servers for over a decade, crazy!

- $400/mo - similarly added Lifecycle Policies to my Cloudflare R2 bucket for Photo AI, pics are automatically put in cheaper Infrequent Access after 90 days, there was years of photos in there so this reduced the R2 bill from $1,200/mo to $800/mo

- $118/mo - Claude analyzed all my Cloudflare Domain registrations, lots of domains I didn't use and didn't make sense to keep paying for, lots of things that also don't really make sense anymore in a post-AGI world, renewals for .io TLD are now $50/year which adds up fast!

- $100/mo - Claude also analyzed my Claude subscription (yes!) and discovered I don't even use the Max 20x plan limits, so I downgraded from $200/mo to $100/mo

Even including Photo AI, I have now cut my costs by 90% from last year, getting me close to my biz expenses amount from a decade ago when I started building things

Costs slowly creep up over the years and you don't realize all the things you're spending on but AI is nice to help you figure all that out (also in your personal life!)
hits.hook: 💸 Update: My total biz expenses have now dropped to just ~$300/mo!  This is to run all my websites/apps serving per year
hits.quote_note: @levelsio: ✨ I replaced all these SaaS with my own vibe coded now, so about $25,000/mo savings:  - Weather API  (853,982)
hits.draft_en:
Pieter Levels cut his business expenses to about $300/month for sites serving 20,000 paying customers and 252M visitors a year, with Claude Code finding the savings. 381k views, 3.8k bookmarks.

The biggest wins were boring: cheaper video models cut his GPU bill from $36k to $7k a month, backup versioning trimmed to 30 days took Backblaze from $1,200 to $26, unused domains dropped, and even his Claude plan went from $200 to $100 after it checked his real usage.

Try it this week: export your bills and ask an agent to find what you stopped using.
hits.video_tip: 10s: a stack of invoices, then a bar chart dropping from $36k to $7k, caption 'my agent audited my bills'.

hits.draft_en:

hits.text:
This year we saw the 3 most important AI releases ever:

• Grok Bot
• Opus 5.5
• Hermes Agent

The most powerful pieces of technology we've ever used

All 3 when used on conjunction can build you a business, make you revenue, and automate all the pieces of your life you don't enjoy

If you haven't worked these 3 into your regular workflow yet, carve out some time this week to do it

Give Grok Bot all your tasks. Use Opus 5.5 to build incredible applications. Have Hermes agent manage all of your devices

If integrated into your life properly you can spend WAY more time doing what you love and WAY less time doing what you hate

Not using these yet should be a massive red flag

outsiders.name: Matt Pocock
outsiders.text:
We need to reconsider our priors on code readability.

Humans, compared to agents, are pretty slow at understanding large quantities of text. So in the old days, readability was important so the human could efficiently grok what was going on.

So readability now comes down to:

1. Can a human, if needed, jump in and understand the code
2. Does the code use the same domain language as the human describing the code?

1 helps with observability and the occasional spot checks you need to do on important PR's. 2 helps the agent translate the words you use into code changes.

In other words, readability is now a nicety, not a necessity.

The way agents 'read' code is different - good agents are all about gathering data about how the code works. They'll prod around with it, execute parts of it.

So 'readability' to agents really means 'verifiability'. How easy it is to mess about with that code to see it working.

Let's take this scenario:

- You have a huge module in your codebase that uses all sorts of complex performance tricks
- It has 100% test coverage

A talented human would need an hour or two to get comfortable working in that module.

An agent needs zero time. They verify it with the tests, poke about a bit, and they're good to go.

The takeaways:

- When judging a module (or a codebase), don't think about how easy the code is to read
- Instead, think about how easy it is to verify
- Design your codebase so modules can be tested and verified independently
- Feel free to sacrifice a bit of readability for performance
- Cyclomatic complexity and function size don't matter to agents

virals.angle: Let an agent audit your bills
virals.draft_en:
Pieter Levels got his business expenses down to about $300/month, serving 20,000 paying customers, and Claude Code found most of the savings.

None of it was clever. It was stuff that crept up:
1. An old video model costing $29k/month more than newer ones
2. Backups kept forever, $1,200/month down to $26 with a 30-day policy
3. Domains he wasn't using
4. A $200 AI plan when his usage fit the $100 one

Export your invoices, hand them to an agent, and ask: what am I paying for that I don't use?
virals.video_tip: 10s: invoices fanned on a desk, then a chart dropping 90%, caption 'my agent found $34k/mo'.

virals.angle: Run the company on voice notes
virals.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's agent stack got 12.8k bookmarks in a day, and most of it is copyable.

The flow: voice note to Grok Bot, an agent grills the idea before anything is built, the spec lands in Linear, agents design four versions of each screen, a fleet builds in separate worktrees, Sentry errors become fix PRs, and a 7am job checks yesterday's funnel.

The habits matter more than the tools:
1. One agent per platform
2. Cheap model for triage, best model for anything that ships
3. Every mistake becomes a skill
4. Every agent writes a 5-line log at night
virals.inspired_by: @gregisenberg agent-managed company (519k, 12.8k bookmarks) + 'voice notes and inference' (25k) + @mattpocockuk skills repo nearly most-starred (55k)
virals.video_tip: 12s: voice note waveform, then a timeline idea, spec, screens, PR, preview, caption 'what I do now is talk'.

virals.angle: Readable code now means verifiable code
virals.draft_en:
Matt Pocock made a point worth sitting with: agents don't read code like we do. They poke at it, run it, and check the tests.

So a messy, performance-tuned module with full test coverage takes a human hours to get comfortable with, and an agent almost no time.

If agents write most of your code, ask a different question about each module: how easy is it to verify? Independent tests and clear domain names now matter more than short functions.
virals.inspired_by: @mattpocockuk readability is now verifiability (97k, 869 bookmarks) + @thsottiaux agents incredible yet frustrating (1.13M)
virals.video_tip: 10s: a dense module on screen, then an agent running the tests green in seconds, caption 'agents verify, they don't read'.

virals.draft_en:
Two things this week: Alex Finn says Qwen 3.8 running on a laptop feels like Opus 4.6 with no limits, and Moonshot posted Kimi K3.1 Pro weights that need about 1.5 TB just to store.

The practical split for builders:
1. Small local model for drafts, triage and private data
2. Frontier model for anything that ships

Test the local one on your own tasks before trusting anyone's benchmark comparison, including Alex's.
virals.inspired_by: @AlexFinn Qwen 3.8 local (102k, 1.3k bookmarks) + @kimmonismus Kimi K3.1 Pro weights (14k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: laptop with wifi off still answering, then a cost card 'local for triage, frontier for ship', caption 'route by job'.

virals.angle: Agents that make the phone call
virals.draft_en:
The agent demos getting the most views right now aren't chat. They're errands: research the best doctors nearby, call them, and book an appointment. Shop, order, track, and return what you don't want.

Apple is opening Siri to multi-step app actions too.

If you build a product, ask whether an agent can complete the main task without a human clicking through. That's quickly becoming the new usability test.
virals.inspired_by: @elonmusk Grok Bot calls and books doctors (3.26M, 2.52M) + Grok Bot shopping (1.0M) + @mgorbach Siri developer preview (561k) + @yoheinakajima multi-step Siri (4k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: agent dialing a clinic, a calendar slot filling in, caption 'the agent made the call'.

virals_narrative: Window Tue Nov 3 ~11:15 CT through Wed Nov 4 ~11:15 CT. The watchlist was led by Greg Isenberg's full agent-run company stack (519k views, 12.8k bookmarks, the most-saved watchlist post in weeks): voice notes in, agents grilling ideas, designing, building in parallel worktrees, fixing Sentry errors and logging nightly. Pieter Levels followed with his expenses falling to about $300/month after Claude Code audited his GPU, servers, backups, domains and even his own AI plan (381k, 3.8k bookmarks). Alex Finn's local Qwen 3.8 laptop video (102k) rode frustration with usage limits. Outside the watchlist, Grok Bot errand demos (phone calls, doctor booking, shopping) and Apple's Siri app-actions preview pushed agents that finish tasks. Builders talked about how code changes when agents are the readers (Matt Pocock), OpenAI buying Pierre for Codex, and Anthropic's FlashProve for verifying which model produced a response; GPT-6.2 rumors pointed at Friday. The meta: show the stack and the receipts, let agents audit costs, design code to be verified, and make products an agent can complete end to end.

scout_meta.method_note: Data came from the X API read connector (Grok Bot public read access): full-archive search from:<handle> -is:retweet -is:reply from 2026-11-03 17:15 UTC (Nov 3 11:15 CST), long texts from note_tweet, quoted posts fetched by id. View counts are impression_count at ~11:15-11:25 CT Nov 4. Outsiders from account-group searches (AI labs, AI builders) plus posts quoted by watchlist hits, all since Nov 2 ~11:15 CT; political and non-AI posts were left out. Posts already on the board were excluded. Duplicate reposts and off-lane posts are kept as hits but flagged skip in drafts.
